**Verdict: the proposed answer 1/4 is wrong.** The argument has a flaw, and a simple construction beats 1/4.

**Lemma 1 is false as stated.** A square S can have holes on its north and south sides at the same time. The edges touching those holes are opposite edges of S, and they do not intersect. The lemma only holds for adjacent sides, since those edges share a corner. The distinctness count in Section 3 depends on this false lemma, so the upper bound h_n ≤ n/4 is not established.

**A better construction.** Let P be a large rectangle of cells, and let the holes be exactly the cells (x, y) with x and y both odd, away from the frame. Keep a frame of P cells around the outside so that no hole touches the outer boundary.

- Every other cell belongs to P. Each row with even y and each column with even x is fully in P, so P is edge-connected.
- Each hole is a single unit square. Its four neighbours have an even coordinate, so they lie in P, and each hole is a bounded component of the complement.
- Holes are two units apart in both directions. Two holes never share an edge or a corner, so their boundaries are pairwise disjoint and disjoint from the outer boundary.

In this pattern the holes have density 1/4 and P has density 3/4 of the area, so h/n → 1/3. Padding the frame adjusts n to any large value with negligible loss, so h_n/n is at least about 1/3 along a sequence of n tending to infinity.

Since 1/3 > 1/4, the limit cannot be 1/4. The construction in Section 4 uses spacing 3 and reaches only 1/4. Spacing 2 is enough to be valid and gives a higher ratio.

VERDICT: REJECT
CONFIDENCE: 5
